hints: Write the outer electron arrangement for P, S and Cl as $3s^2 3p^x$ and find x from the Period 3 group number.
Remember that p orbitals fill singly first, so count how many 3p electrons remain unpaired for 3, 4 and 5 electrons.
walkthrough:
Find the 3p electron count from position in Period 3**
P is Group 15, S is Group 16, Cl is Group 17. After $3s^2$, the extra electrons go into 3p. So P has $3s^2 3p^3$, S has $3s^2 3p^4$ and Cl has $3s^2 3p^5$. That gives 3, 4, 5 electrons in 3p.

Apply Hund's rule for unpaired electrons**
The three 3p orbitals each take one electron first. P with 3 electrons has one in each orbital, so 3 unpaired. S with 4 electrons must pair up one orbital, leaving 2 unpaired. Cl with 5 electrons must pair up two orbitals, leaving 1 unpaired.

Final answer: Number of electrons in 3p: P = 3, S = 4, Cl = 5.
Total number of unpaired electrons: P = 3, S = 2, Cl = 1.

hints: Recall that first ionisation removes one electron from one mole of gaseous atoms to form gaseous 1+ ions.
walkthrough:
Build the ionisation equation**
Start with one gaseous P atom, $\text{P(g)}$. Remove one electron to give $\text{P}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$. Both species must be gaseous because first ionisation energy is defined for isolated gaseous atoms.
Final answer: $\text{P(g)} \rightarrow \text{P}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$

hints: Compare the three choices with P (1060) and Cl (1260) and decide which value shows the expected dip at S.
Think about how nuclear charge changes from P to S to Cl with the same shielding.
Recall why S is lower than P despite higher nuclear charge, by looking at the pairing in your table from (a)(i).
Link lower nuclear attraction for S versus Cl to easier removal of the outer electron.
walkthrough:
Choose the value that dips below P**
Across Period 3, ionisation energy generally rises, but S dips below P. P is 1060 and Cl is 1260, so S must be below 1060. Only $1000\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ fits. 1160 would be a smooth rise, 1320 would be above Cl, both are wrong.

Compare S with Cl using nuclear charge**
From S to Cl, protons increase from 16 to 17 while electrons are added to the same shell, so shielding stays almost the same. Cl therefore exerts a stronger nuclear attraction on its outer electrons, so more energy is needed to remove one. That is why S is well below Cl.

Explain why S is below P despite more protons**
S does have one more proton than P, which alone would suggest higher ionisation energy. But look back at (a)(i): S has $3p^4$ with a paired pair, while P has $3p^3$ with three unpaired electrons. The two electrons sharing one orbital repel each other by spin-pair repulsion.

Tie it together**
That repulsion makes the paired electron in S easier to remove, outweighing the extra proton. So S drops below P, and is also well below Cl where nuclear charge dominates.

Final answer: $1000\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
S has lower first ionisation energy than P and Cl because of least nuclear attraction on outer electrons; Cl has stronger nuclear attraction than S.
Cl has greater nuclear charge than S, with similar shielding, so holds electrons more strongly.
S has greater nuclear charge than P but has two electrons paired in one 3p orbital, so spin-pair repulsion makes removal easier.

hints: Start from the neutral P atom configuration and add three electrons to complete the third shell.
walkthrough:
Add three electrons to phosphorus**
Neutral P is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^3$. Adding $3e^-$ to form $\text{P}^{3-}$ fills the 3p subshell to $3p^6$. So the full configuration is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6$, the same as argon.
Final answer: $1\text{s}^{2} 2\text{s}^{2} 2\text{p}^{6} 3\text{s}^{2} 3\text{p}^{6}$

hints: Note all three ions have the same electron arrangement, so compare their proton numbers: P (15), S (16), Cl (17).
Think about how increasing protons with identical shielding changes the pull on the same number of electrons.
walkthrough:
State the trend**
$\text{P}^{3-}$, $\text{S}^{2-}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ are isoelectronic, all with 18 electrons. Going from $\text{P}^{3-}$ to $\text{S}^{2-}$ to $\text{Cl}^{-}$, the radius gets smaller.

Explain with protons pulling the same electrons**
The electron count and shielding are identical, but proton number rises: 15, 16, 17. More protons means greater nuclear attraction on the same outer shell, so the electron cloud is drawn in more tightly and the ion shrinks.

Final answer: Ionic radius decreases from $\text{P}^{3-}$ to $\text{Cl}^{-}$.
Increasing nuclear charge with the same shielding gives increased attraction of outer electrons for the nucleus, pulling them closer.

hints: For test 1, decide whether bromine, a stronger oxidising agent than chlorine, can displace chloride.
For test 2, recall that concentrated sulfuric acid with NaCl gives HCl fumes but no coloured oxidation products, unlike with NaBr or NaI.
For test 3, recall the characteristic colour of the silver halide precipitate for chloride.
walkthrough:
Test 1 with bromine**
Bromine is below chlorine in Group 17, so it is a weaker oxidising agent and cannot oxidise $\text{Cl}^{-}$ to $\text{Cl}_{2}$. No displacement occurs, so you just see the orange or brown colour of the added $\text{Br}_{2}$(aq), with no change.

Test 2 with concentrated sulfuric acid**
Concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ reacts with $\text{Cl}^{-}$ to give HCl gas only, which is colourless. Chloride is not strong enough a reducing agent to reduce sulfur to $\text{SO}_{2}$ or $\text{H}_{2}\text{S}$, so there is no visible colour change in solution.

Test 3 with silver nitrate**
$\text{Ag}^{+}$(aq) + $\text{Cl}^{-}$(aq) gives $\text{AgCl}$, which is seen as a white precipitate. This is the classic positive test for chloride.

Final answer: Test 1 ($\text{Br}_{2}$): no visible reaction OR stays orange / brown / yellow solution.
Test 2 (conc. $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$): no visible reaction OR solution remains colourless.
Test 3 (dil. $\text{AgNO}_{3}$): white precipitate forms.

hints: Think about what low melting and boiling points tell you about the strength of forces between molecules.
Think about what vigorous reaction with water to give an acidic solution tells you about chloride covalent compounds.
walkthrough:
Use the melting and boiling points**
Melting at $1^{\circ}\text{C}$ and boiling at $106^{\circ}\text{C}$ are very low compared with giant lattices. That fits discrete $\text{POCl}_{3}$ molecules held together only by weak van der Waals forces, which need little energy to separate.

Use the reaction with water**
A vigorous reaction forming misty fumes and an acidic solution is typical hydrolysis of a covalent chloride, like $\text{PCl}_{5}$ or $\text{SiCl}_{4}$, producing HCl. Ionic or giant structures would simply dissolve, not hydrolyse so vigorously.

Final answer: Low melting and boiling points suggest weak intermolecular / van der Waals forces between simple molecules.
Vigorous reaction with water to give acidic solution suggests hydrolysis.

hints: Hydrolysis of $\text{POCl}_{3}$ gives phosphoric acid $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ plus HCl, so balance Cl with water.
walkthrough:
Construct the hydrolysis equation**
Each Cl becomes HCl, so 3 Cl need $3\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to supply H and O for $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4} + 3\text{HCl}$. Check atoms: P 1, O 4, H 6, Cl 3 on both sides, so it balances.
Final answer: $\text{POCl}_{3} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4} + 3\text{HCl}$

hints: Count shared pairs: P forms one double bond to O (4 electrons) plus three single bonds to Cl (6 electrons).
Then add lone pairs so O and each Cl each have 8 outer electrons, giving 32 outer electrons in total.
walkthrough:
Draw the bonding electrons**
Put P in the centre. Show one pair of dots and crosses in each P-Cl overlap (3 single bonds) and two shared pairs in the P-O overlap (double bond). That uses 10 bonding electrons around P, allowed as P can expand its octet.

Complete the octets**
Give O two lone pairs and each Cl three lone pairs using dots for one atom and crosses for the other. Count: bonding 10 + O lone pairs 4 + 3 x Cl lone pairs 18 = 32 outer electrons. Show outer shells only.

Final answer: Dot-and-cross diagram shows P sharing 2 electrons with each Cl (3 single bonds) and 4 electrons with O (double bond).
O has 2 lone pairs (4 electrons) and each Cl has 3 lone pairs (6 electrons each), total 32 outer shell electrons with correct dots and crosses for shared pairs.

hints: Start the definition with the amount formed: one mole of compound.
State what it is formed from: elements in their standard states under standard conditions.
walkthrough:
Amount and process**
The key amount is one mole of the compound being formed. That is what $\Delta H_{f}$ refers to.

Starting materials and conditions**
It is formed directly from its elements, each in their standard state (their normal physical state at 100 kPa and 298 K), with all substances in standard states.
Final answer: Enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its constituent elements in their standard states.

hints: Write the enthalpy change of the reaction $2\text{PCl}_{3} + \text{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{POCl}_{3}$ using $\Delta H_{r} = \Sigma \Delta H_{f}(products) - \Sigma \Delta H_{f}(reactants)$.
Then equate that $\Delta H_{r}$ to bonds broken minus bonds formed, where the only net change is breaking O=O (+496) and forming two P=O bonds.
walkthrough:
Find $\Delta H_{r}$ from formation data**
$$\Delta H_{r} = 2\Delta H_{f}(\text{POCl}_{3}) - [2\Delta H_{f}(\text{PCl}_{3}) + 0]$$
$$\Delta H_{r} = 2(-592) - 2(-289) = -1184 + 578 = -606\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$ for the equation as written.

Relate to O=O broken and P=O formed**
P-Cl bonds cancel because both sides have six P-Cl bonds. Net: break $\text{O=O}$ (+496) and make $2 \times \text{P=O}$. So: $$-606 = +496 - 2E_{\text{P=O}}$$ Rearranging: $$2E_{\text{P=O}} = 496 + 606 = 1102$$ $$E_{\text{P=O}} = +551\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
